title: AWS Well-Architected Framework
learningObjective: Describe the Well-Architected Framework and its six pillars, and tell the pillars apart.
foundation: The Well-Architected Framework is AWS's set of best practices for designing and running workloads in the cloud.
It has six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability.
The free AWS Well-Architected Tool lets you review a workload against these best practices.
engineer: Operational excellence: perform operations as code, make frequent small reversible changes, refine procedures, anticipate failure, learn from operational events.

Security: strong identity foundation, traceability, security at all layers, automate security best practices, protect data in transit and at rest, keep people away from data, prepare for security events.
Reliability: automatically recover from failure, test recovery procedures, scale horizontally, stop guessing capacity, manage change through automation.
Performance efficiency: democratise advanced technologies, go global in minutes, use serverless architectures, experiment more often, consider mechanical sympathy.
Cost optimization: implement cloud financial management, adopt a consumption model, measure overall efficiency, stop spending on undifferentiated heavy lifting, analyse and attribute expenditure.
Sustainability: understand your impact, establish goals, maximise utilisation, adopt more efficient hardware and software, use managed services, reduce downstream impact.

animation.caption: Open 'Well-Architected pillars' and match concerns to pillars.

example.title: A review before launch
body: Before launching, a team runs a Well-Architected review in the Well-Architected Tool. It finds single-AZ databases (reliability), no MFA on admin users (security) and oversized instances (cost), and fixes them.

prerequisites: An AWS account (use an IAM Identity Center user, not root)
permissions: Read-only access to explore; least-privilege permissions to change resources
limits: Conceptual objective: explore in the console; no configuration limits are tested
portal: AWS Well-Architected Tool > Define workload > Start review.

steps: Pick each requirement, choose an answer and run it.
Read why the best answer fits.
failureScenarios: Choosing by name instead of requirement
lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.fix: Rightsize, adopt the consumption model, attribute spend.

comparisons.difference: Five pillars (reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence, performance efficiency); AWS adds sustainability as a sixth pillar.

misconceptions.reality: It is about using resources efficiently to meet requirements; cost has its own pillar.

misconceptions.myth: The framework is a paid service.
misconceptions.reality: The framework and the Well-Architected Tool are free.

architectureDecisions: Review workloads regularly, not only before launch.

verification.notes: Drafted by AI and checked against the linked official documentation. Not yet reviewed by a human subject-matter expert.

walkthrough.subtitle: Review one workload against the six pillars and see what each pillar is really asking.

steps.label: Is it good?
steps.title: Is this design any good?
body: Your web shop works. But will it survive a failure? Is it secure? Are you paying too much?
"It works" is not the same as "it is well designed". You need a checklist.

steps.label: The framework
steps.title: AWS's checklist: the Well-Architected Framework
body: The Well-Architected Framework is AWS's set of best practices and questions for designing and running workloads in the cloud.
The free AWS Well-Architected Tool in the console walks you through the questions and records the risks it finds.

callout.text: It is guidance and a review process, not a service that changes your resources.

steps.label: Ops + Security
steps.title: Pillars 1-2: run it well and keep it safe
body: Operational excellence asks: can you run, monitor and improve this? Think operations as code, small reversible changes, and learning from incidents.
Security asks: are data and systems protected? Think strong identities, traceability, encryption, and security at every layer.

steps.label: Reliability + Perf
steps.title: Pillars 3-4: keep working and stay fast
body: Reliability asks: does it recover from failure and meet demand? Think multiple AZs, automatic recovery, and tested backups.
Performance efficiency asks: are you using the right resources, efficiently? Think the right instance type, serverless, caching, and going global.

steps.label: Cost + Sustainability
steps.title: Pillars 5-6: spend wisely and waste less
body: Cost optimization asks: are you paying only for what delivers value? Think rightsizing, the right pricing model, and turning off idle resources.
Sustainability asks: are you reducing environmental impact? Think high utilisation, efficient hardware, and managed services.

steps.label: Review
steps.title: Case: a review before launch
body: The review finds a database in one AZ, so reliability is at risk. Admins without MFA is a security risk. Oversized servers running at 5% CPU is a cost risk, and a sustainability one too.
Each finding belongs to the pillar whose question it fails.

callout.text: Reliability = recovers from failure. Performance efficiency = right resources for speed. Cost optimization = paying less for the same value. Sustainability = less energy and waste.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Six pillars, six questions
body: Use the question each pillar asks to place any scenario.
recap: Operational excellence: can we run and improve it?
Reliability: does it recover and meet demand?
Performance efficiency: right resources, used efficiently?
Cost optimization: paying only for value?
